Saying
SAY-ing
n. (rendering Hebrew dabar, Greek logos/rhēma)
A verbal noun from say, Saxon secgan, to utter. In the Authorized Version a saying is a definite utterance treated as a unit — a word that can be kept, pondered, believed, or rejected as a whole, and which is often quoted back later because it was remembered.

Biblical Definition

A saying in Scripture is a word that has been fixed in the memory and can be handed on. Mary's response to what she could not yet understand is the model: “his mother kept all these sayings in her heart” (Luke 2:51) — not solved, not explained, kept. The Lord Jesus closes the Sermon on the Mount by making His sayings the foundation a life is built on or ruined for want of: “whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man” (Matthew 7:24). John records how a saying can travel and be corrupted in transit: “Then went this saying abroad among the brethren, that that disciple should not die: yet Jesus said not unto him” (John 21:23) — the report circulated, and the evangelist corrects it by returning to what was actually said. And Paul stamps five sayings in the Pastorals with an apostolic seal, of which the first is the sum of the gospel: “This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1 Timothy 1:15). These faithful sayings are the earliest confessional formulae of the church — compact, memorable, doctrinally exact — and they show that the apostolic church catechised by fixed forms of sound words, not by impressions.

Webster 1828 Definition

An expression, a declaration, a maxim uttered and remembered; in Scripture, the sayings of Christ that a wise man builds upon, the sayings Mary kept in her heart, and the faithful sayings the apostle stamps as worthy of all acceptation.

expand to see more

SAYING, n. 1. An expression; a sentence uttered; a declaration.

2. A proverbial expression; a maxim; as, it is a common saying.

3. That which is repeated and remembered as the word of another.

4. From say, Saxon secgan, to utter, to speak.

5. In Scripture, a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptation, 1 Tim. 1; his mother kept all these sayings in her heart, Luke 2.

Key Scripture

1 Timothy 1:15 — "This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief."

Matthew 7:24 — "Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:"

Luke 2:51 — "And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject unto them: but his mother kept all these sayings in her heart."

John 21:23 — "Then went this saying abroad among the brethren, that that disciple should not die: yet Jesus said not unto him, He shall not die; but, If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee?"

Modern Corruption

The sayings of Christ are separated from His person and His atoning work, so that He is honoured as a teacher of maxims while the doctrine that gives the maxims their force is quietly dropped.

expand to see more

Nineteenth-century liberalism produced a Jesus who was a teacher of timeless sayings and little else — the Sermon on the Mount without the cross, the golden rule without the wrath it saves from. The same instinct persists wherever the words of Christ are printed in red and treated as the real gospel while the epistles that expound His death are treated as Paul's overlay. But the Lord's sayings will not survive the separation. Matthew 7:24 makes obedience to His sayings the difference between a house that stands and one that falls, and the sentence is a claim to divine authority that no mere teacher could make. Strip out who He is and the sayings become an intolerable moral burden, which is exactly what they were designed to be for the self-righteous and never were for those who came to Him poor in spirit.

The opposite corruption is the endless multiplication of sayings that God never said. John 21:23 is instructive because it shows how quickly a report can circulate among believers in a form the Lord never uttered, and how an apostle handles it — not by celebrating the tradition but by correcting it against the actual words. The modern equivalents are the “God told me” culture of the charismatic movement and the pious slogans that circulate as though they were scripture. The principle to recover is the apostolic one: fixed, faithful sayings, tested and confessed, held fast in the form of sound words, and everything else measured by them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dabar, a word or matter spoken; 'imrah, an utterance or speech; Greek logos, a word or discourse, and rhēma, a spoken saying.

expand to see more

Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, saying, or matter; the same noun covers the thing said and the thing done.

Hebrew 'imrah (H565) — an utterance, speech, commandment; frequent in Psalm 119 for God's word as promise.

Greek logos (G3056) — a word, account, or discourse; rendered saying where a definite utterance is in view.

Greek rhēma (G4487) — a spoken word, a saying; “they understood not this saying” (Luke 9:45).

Greek pistos ho logos — “faithful is the word,” the apostolic formula introducing the five faithful sayings of the Pastorals.

Usage

"Of the gospel in one confessional sentence: This is a faithful saying... that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1 Timothy 1:15)."

"Of the foundation of an obedient life: whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them (Matthew 7:24)."

"Of a report corrected against the actual word: yet Jesus said not unto him (John 21:23)."
